title: EXPLAINER: Why is the Trump administration pushing for Pax Silica?

blocks.text: In the days leading up to US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines, protesters have rallied against him and the planned Pax Silica initiative — but why has his administration kept pushing for the project?
In a report from GMA News Feed, the Pax Silica project is a flagship effort of the US to strengthen AI ecosystems.
According to the US Department of State, the Pax Silica project wants to secure the supply chain for creating a Super Intelligence (SI) by developing an “economic consensus” among allies,
Included in the supply chain are the materials and resources needed for AI, including critical minerals, energy, manufacturing, semiconductors, and other infrastructure like data centers.

The US think tank Council on Foreign Relations believes that the Pax Silica project is an attempt to get resources to develop advanced AI technology. Others believe that the US wants to maintain its superiority in AI development.

“US still considers itself as retaining superiority in terms of the development of these AI tools and software. However, there are serious concerns by the US, on the fact that China can acquire technology and know-how to develop their own and quickly catch up, so essentially gaining an edge in the AI race,” said UP Department of Political Science Senior Lecturer Matteo Piasentini.
Piasentini said that the US was using Pax Silica as “tactical practice” to show its dominance to China. The US was also making use of the Philippines for cheap labor to manufacture AI parts.

“To use a metaphor, it’s great powers waving shiny objects in the international system, and creating incentives for, let's say, smaller states to explore, right? Possibilities, opportunities, while, you know, putting question marks against, on the other part, on the counterpart or the other power that used to or that thought would retain dominance over certain sectors of the economy,” he said.

According to the US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, the US and China saw Southeast Asia as an area of competition. Among ASEAN members, the Philippines and Singapore signed the Pax Silica initiative.

Meanwhile, seven countries from Southeast Asia, namely Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Viet Nam and Brunei, are part of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization --- an AI initiative by China. However, other parts of Southeast Asia are unlikely to choose sides.

“I don't think anyone in the United States is naive enough to think that Southeast Asian countries will choose between Pax Silica and the Chinese initiative. Southeast Asian countries, apart from the Philippines and a few other exceptions, pride themselves on their equidistance,” Piasentini said.
The Philippines signed the Pax Silica declaration in April 2026. With this are plans to establish the Pax Silica Economic Security Zone at the Luzon Economic Corridor.

The US Department of State said that this will be a staging point for the hub and industrial activities. Initial reports said that the project included the processing of critical minerals to make components of high-tech AI conductors,

However, many have decried the Pax Silica initiative, fearing possible displacement of local indigenous people. Many have also feared the possible impacts that the initiative could have on the environment.

While the government has reassured that Pax Silica will have minimal negative effects to the local community and the environment, it did not dissuade hundreds of protesters from questioning who will truly benefit from the AI hub at the end of the day.
Piasentini urged the government to ensure that the process remained transparent.

“The administration must insist on having as much as possible, a process, ensuring as much as possible, a process of implementation and negotiation that is transparent and inclusive, even I would say, at the cost of sacrificing expediency and urgency,” Piasentini said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News
